name: CA Compromise Scenarios
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What Actually Goes Wrong, Step by Step
lesson.summary: Walking through realistic sequences of how a certificate authority compromise unfolds shows why signature validity alone cannot catch misissuance, and why detection mechanisms like certificate transparency were built.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter categorized certificate authority vulnerabilities in the abstract: process failure, technical breach, insider risk, coercion. It helps to trace one scenario through from start to finish to see why these failures are dangerous in practice rather than just in theory. Take the technical breach case, closely modeled on what actually happened to DigiNotar in 2011. An attacker gains unauthorized access to a certificate authority's issuance systems, the software that actually generates and signs certificates. From inside, the attacker requests certificates for domains they do not own or control, and because they are operating through the certificate authority's own legitimate signing infrastructure, the resulting certificates carry entirely valid signatures traceable up a completely intact chain to a trusted root.

At this point, nothing about the certificate itself looks wrong to a browser. The signature verifies. The chain resolves to a root sitting in the trust store. Every mechanical check described in earlier chapters passes. The only thing wrong is a fact no signature can encode: this certificate authority should never have issued this particular certificate to this particular requester. That gap between mechanically valid and factually correct is precisely why the attacker can then use the fraudulent certificate to impersonate the real domain in a man in the middle attack, intercepting traffic that victims believe is securely encrypted directly with the legitimate site, while it is actually being decrypted and re-encrypted by the attacker in between.

A different scenario involves domain validation weaknesses rather than a full systems breach. Many certificate authorities validate domain control through automated means, such as sending an email to an address associated with the domain or checking for a specific record the requester was asked to place in DNS. If an attacker can intercept that email, through a separate mail server compromise, or manipulate DNS responses through a routing attack, they can satisfy the validation check without ever breaching the certificate authority itself, and walk away with a legitimately issued certificate for a domain they do not actually control.

What eventually exposed the DigiNotar breach, and what has since become a standard defense, is certificate transparency: a system requiring certificate authorities to publish every certificate they issue to public, append only logs that anyone can audit. A domain owner can monitor these logs for certificates issued for their own domain and notice, often within hours, if one appears that they never requested. This does not prevent misissuance, but it converts an invisible failure into a tamper evident one, borrowing the same core idea from earlier in this book: append only, publicly checkable logs make it much harder for a bad certificate to exist quietly and be used without anyone noticing. The lesson across every compromise scenario is consistent: a chain of valid signatures proves internal consistency, not external truth, and closing that gap requires transparency mechanisms layered on top of the certificate system itself, not just better cryptography inside it.
